This gestation time has been measured at 26 days [tg = 26 days] when females are maintained at a stable core body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], a physiological condition typical of this species' active phase. The brevity of this intrauterine development, common among many murid rodents, places a premium on rapid postnatal growth. Within just over three weeks, the dependent young undergo a dramatic transformation, and the time since birth at weaning is 23 days after birth [tx = 23 days after birth] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. At this point, the weanlings have achieved a wet weight at weaning of 25 grams [Wwx = 25 grams], representing a more than fivefold increase from their birth mass. This rapid pre-weaning growth trajectory underscores the efficiency of maternal lactation in this species.

This differential maturation rate is a common pattern in rodent biology, often linked to sexual selection and the competitive advantages conferred by a larger body size in males. The values, recorded in stable laboratory colonies, provide a baseline for understanding the species' reproductive physiology under optimal conditions.

This longevity, which is considerable for a rodent of its size, is likely an adaptation to the unpredictable and arid environments of North Africa where the species is endemic. A longer lifespan allows for multiple reproductive opportunities across several seasons, buffering against years of poor resource availability. The ultimate wet weight, or maximum adult body mass, recorded for this species is 185 grams [Wwi = 185 grams], a size that places it among the larger members of the genus Meriones. This substantial body mass supports prolonged survival and the ability to store fat reserves necessary for enduring periods of food scarcity.
